query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: We hypothesize that applying moderate-temperature forging (about 0.5–0.6Tm) with a forging strain of 0.3–0.4 to eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), followed by a short low-temperature anneal, will refine and partially spheroidize the B2/fcc lamellar microstructure, reduce stress concentrations at colony boundaries, and thereby improve both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility beyond the as-cast lamellar-colony baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast dual-phase EHEA with lamellar fcc/B2 colonies exhibiting limited room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Warm forging to moderate plastic strains in the 0.5–0.6Tm temperature range, followed by a brief low-temperature annealing cycle for stress relief.
generation.conditions: Forging at 800–900 °C to a total strain of approximately 0.3–0.4, cooling, and a short (e.g., 600–700 °C) anneal under inert or vacuum conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Lamellar refinement, partial spheroidization of B2/fcc phases, and reduced high-angle boundary facets that otherwise serve as crack-initiation sites.
generation.mechanism: Moderately warm forging breaks up coarse lamellar boundaries and introduces beneficial dislocation substructures, while a short post-forging anneal relieves internal stresses. These combined microstructural changes minimize microcrack nucleation and growth at colony interfaces and enhance the alloy’s ability to accommodate plastic strain without fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: In tensile tests at room temperature, strength remains comparable or somewhat enhanced relative to the as-cast baseline, while elongation to failure increases by multiple percentage points, reflecting delayed microcrack initiation and slower crack propagation.
generation.baseline: As-cast EHEA with well-defined lamellar B2/fcc colonies that show high strength but limited ductility at room temperature.
generation.boundary: This approach is most effective when forging temperature and strain are sufficient to refine lamellae without causing excessive grain coarsening. Extremely high forging strains or forging temperatures above ~0.6Tm could degrade the beneficial microstructure and offset any ductility gains.
generation.uncertainty: Exact forging temperature, strain, and subsequent annealing must be optimized. Inappropriate processing parameters could result in excessive grain growth, retained stress concentrations, or phase instability that negate the intended benefits.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample sets of the same EHEA composition and as-cast lamellar microstructure. Subject one set to the warm forging (0.3–0.4 strain at 0.5–0.6Tm) plus short low-temperature anneal. Retain the other set in the as-cast condition as a control. Perform comparative room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation, and observe fracture morphology.
measurements: Microstructural characterization by SEM/TEM to confirm the presence or absence of lamellar refinement and spheroidization.
Localized microcrack initiation and distribution, especially around colony boundaries, by post-failure fractography.
Tensile properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If forging and short annealing fail to reduce boundary microcracking or produce no improvement in ductility (or significantly lower the strength relative to the as-cast state), the hypothesis is invalidated.

To verify this novel alloy design strategy, an industrial scale AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 ingot of ~2.5 kg in weight was prepared, as shown in Fig. 1a . The bulk AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy exhibited an excellent castability with few casting defects, significantly differentiating with other bulk HEAs. The tensile test specimen was machined from the bulk alloy ingot and is shown in Fig. 1b . The cast microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 is shown in Fig. 2a . Even in such a bulk cast ingot, a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure characteristic of eutectic alloys was achieved. The inter-lamellar spacing was about 2 μm. The coupled grown two phases showed a clear compositional contrast, with the regions marked by A in Fig. 2b were rich in Co, Cr and Fe, while the regions marked by B were rich in Al and Ni (detailed compositional information given in Table 1 ). An enlarged microstructure given in Fig. 2c shows that dense nanoscale NiAl-rich precipitates (marked as B II ) occurred in the CoCrFe-rich region. As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . decision.trend: Early work on eutectic AlCoCrFeNi-type high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) with dual-phase B2/fcc lamellar microstructures demonstrated high strength and moderate ductility as-cast, but cold rolling to enhance strength provoked severe ductility loss (PMC4145285). Separately, in a B2-containing high-entropy alloy designed to overcome initial brittleness, solutionizing plus tuneable annealing steps enabled partial transformation from a continuous hard B2 matrix to coherent B2 nanoscale precipitates within a softer matrix, resulting in improved strength–ductility combinations but still not fully resolving low room-temperature ductility and microcrack initiation (PMC5995863). Across these efforts, controlling interphase boundaries and refining microstructure helped but did not consistently prevent microcracking or achieve high tensile elongation at room temperature.
decision.unsolved: Despite attempts at solutionizing, cold rolling, and complex heat treatments that shifted phase volume fractions or lamellar spacings, none have fully prevented microcrack formation at colony boundaries. The core issue—room-temperature brittleness from lamellar interfaces—remains unresolved. A method to mitigate internal boundary stresses without sacrificing bulk strength is still needed.
decision.lever: Apply a moderate-temperature forging process (e.g., ~0.5–0.6Tm) to refine and partially spheroidize the lamellar microstructure, followed by a short low-temperature anneal to relieve internal stresses while maintaining fine scales. Typical forging strains of 0.3–0.4 at around 800–900 °C, followed by a brief anneal near 600–700 °C, can promote controlled boundary relaxation and enhance the colony interface bonding strength.
decision.why: Prior work (PMC4145285, PMC5995863) shows that refining or partially transforming B2/fcc lamellae can boost strength and ductility by mitigating microcrack initiation at interfaces. Moderately warm forging plus short low-temperature annealing can break up sharp boundaries, reduce local stress concentrations, and induce beneficial substructure formation. This approach avoids changing alloy composition while preserving high strength and simultaneously increasing ductility. A falsification experiment would compare tensile cracking and measured ductility in as-cast versus thermomechanically treated EHEA; if microcracking and early fracture remain unchanged despite refined lamellae and boundary stress relief, the hypothesis is disproven.
